text: The ovens were making that low, constant hum. It was 3:17 on Thursday morning, and the air was dense with the smell of yeast and burnt sugar. I wiped flour off my forearms and went to the front counter. Under the glass display case, the same old paperback had been sitting for six weeks now. It was called The Shadow of the Wind. I picked it up. The pages were worn, dog-eared, and felt oddly warmer than the cool air. Normally I’d just toss it in the return bin next to the register, figuring some confused customer had left it. But tonight was different. I opened it to the bookmarked page and a folded square of lined notebook paper fell out and landed on the counter. I hesitated, then opened it up. The handwriting was jagged, hurried, like somebody wrote it in a rush. It said: I know you’re reading it. Keep going. Page 204 changes everything. My heart was hammering against my ribs, a sharp rhythm that cut through the quiet hum of the mixers. I looked around the empty shop, shadows stretched long across the tiled floor. Nobody was there. I looked back at the note, then at the book. My fingers were trembling. I turned to page 204. The text blurred before my eyes. I closed the book, pressed it flat against the counter and reached for my pen.
